Transparency standards are a critical enabler of financial integrity. but their effectiveness lies in their ability to deliver measurable outcomes on the ground. Today, information of exchange on request and common reporting standard have become the most widely used mechanisms for cross-border administrative collaboration in tax matters. However, their effectiveness requires more than just exchanging data. The real challenge today is not the absence of data, but the capacity to convert data into actionable intelligence, which is usable, timely, and directly linked to the enforcement outcomes, rather than a merely standalone compliance exercise. As per the annual Global Forum report 2025, the most significant challenge cited by Global Forum members is timeliness. both in obtaining timely responses to outgoing requests and meeting deadlines for incoming requests. Evidence from CRS and FATCA shows that clear reporting obligations and reciprocity create behavioural change and improve compliance outcomes. India's use of CRS and FATCA data in integration with its own high-quality domestic data for nudge campaigns demonstrates the enforcement value of behavioral intentions, leading to large scale voluntary disclosure of undisclosed foreign income and assets. And this initiative has been internationally recognized, including at the last OECD Global Forum Plenary as a good practice in converting transparency into tangible compliance outcomes. Despite progress, significant gaps and asymmetries persist. All of us have discussed it throughout the day. Challenges remain in the identification of beneficial owners and controlling persons, particularly for trust and complex structures, linking financial accounts to beneficial ownership, ensuring consistent metadata for cross-border wire transfers, and the most discussed, interoperability between trade, tax, and financial data sets. Beneficial ownership transparency is recognized as the biggest challenge by the Global Forum itself. It says nearly half of refuted jurisdictions have yet to ensure adequate, accurate, and up-to-date beneficial ownership information for legal entities, arrangements, and bank accounts. In recent times, we have witnessed exponential growth in crypto asset facilitated money laundering. In the crypto ecosystem, enforcement is hampered by anonymous borderless transfers, offshore exchanges and non-custodial wallets, non-implementation of travel rule requirements, and limited access to off-chain KYC and ownership information. Offshore virtual asset service providers often lack meaningful physical presence with compliance functions and data infrastructure located outside users jurisdictions, which limits the supervisory access and timely information sharing. The current frameworks lack technical standards for information exchange from foreign VSPs as well as the universal participation. Further, the effective use of cross-border information exchange is constrained by legal complexity, including data protection and privacy laws, variations in evidentiary standards, authentication requirements, incompatible digital evidence frameworks, slow MLAT processes taking two to four years on an average in the case of India itself, and inconsistent confidentiality protocols. India believes these challenges can be addressed through enabling data sharing frameworks, digitalization of MLAT processes, defined timelines and accountability, and greater convergence of evidentiary and digital standards for enhancing judicial admissibility, while ensuring data protection and confidentiality safeguards. Mandatory inclusion of standardized entity identifiers and STRs and multilateral legal entity identifier type framework can significantly improve traceability and linkages across databases and jurisdictions. Economic and financial crimes span multiple mandates across tax, financial intelligence, customs, anti-corruption, and enforcement agencies. And therefore, addressing the challenges also require an enhanced institutionalized international coordination mechanism with a focus on harmonization of the standards and inclusiveness, strengthening the scope and effective implementation of international reporting frameworks, and reducing barriers to lawful data sharing. The challenge before us is no longer access to data alone, but equitable access, usability, and the capacity to use data effectively. We are aware that by helping people in member countries to become better at digital forensics or crypto investigations or the use of AI, they will naturally increase the capacity of their country to perform better against illicit financial flows. The challenge, of course, is that those people, when they become good at those jobs, may naturally leave the public sector. However, we would argue that that is not a good reason not to train them in the first place. The last point to make is, and I reflect on the comment made by the colleague from civil society at the back, the importance of operational delivery. It is critical that, when we are discussing how to do better, we have the focus of our minds should be on the victims, whether those are individuals or companies or countries, but we must have in our minds the need to return funds to those victims in order that they can be used properly, as well as to bring offenders to justice. And Interpol stands ready to support our member countries in doing that. Thank you.

Thank you, Mr. Court, for the further sharing of your insights. So I would like to thank all of the panelists and the responded on the panel too for their, you know, sharing really very extensive and practical experience and very concise recommendations. If I may, I would have a very brief summary of some recommendations, also in addition to the recommendations generated from panel one. Relating to the strengthening domestic coordination, so it was mentioned that So firstly, it's very important for the relevant competent authorities to deploy integrated approach. Relating to the international cooperation, there are recommendations on raising awareness, raising of the available communication, cooperation, channels, even among the competent authorities. Secondly, there is also recommendation relating to harmonizing, to harmonize the standard and the norms. So with this, I would like to thank everybody again for the contributions. Thanks.

I thank Ms. Lee, our moderator, for excellently guiding the questions and moderating these two sessions. I also thank our distinguished panelists for their substantive and very outstanding contributions, and for all the delegations for their active participations in the interactive discussion with our panelists. Distinguished delegates, colleagues, with this, I now briefly pause the meeting to allow the podium to be rearranged for the closing segment. Please remain seated. Excellencies, distinguished delegates, we have reached the closing segment of this meeting. I now invite Mr. Naveed Hanif, Assistant Secretary-General for Economic and Social Affairs, to make a statement on behalf of the Under-Secretary-General for Economic Development. Mr. Hanif, you have the floor.

Thank you, Mr. President. And I wish to convey Mr. Lee Jun-hwa's sincere regrets that he could not join you this evening at the closing of the first ever meeting of the Council on Financial Integrity. As we conclude this meeting, one truth stands out clearly. Financial integrity is not a technical aspiration. It is a moral imperative. And a development necessity. I sincerely appreciate the strong engagement and practical focus that shaped today's discussions. As reaffirmed in the Fourth International Conference on Financing for Development, these challenges cannot be addressed by countries acting alone. A loophole in one system becomes a vulnerability for all. The scale of the problem is stark. UNODC estimates that trillions of dollars, around 3% of global GDP, are lost each year through illicit financial flows. At the same time, up to one-tenth of global wealth may be hidden offshore, beyond the reach of tax authorities. These are not abstract figures. They represent schools never built, hospitals never equipped, and opportunities denied to millions. They represent a double theft, of public trust and of the promise of a better future. Financial integrity is therefore a development issue, with direct and measurable consequences for people on the ground. Responding effectively requires more than cooperation. It requires stronger laws, stronger institutions, and of course, stronger enforcement at both national and international levels. Ladies and gentlemen, accountability must extend across the entire financial ecosystem. Those who enable financial crime or turn a blind eye to abusive practices must face effective and punitive sanctions alongside those who commit the crimes themselves. Without this, enforcement will remain incomplete. The SVEA commitment provides a clear roadmap for action. It calls for stronger cross-border cooperation to prosecute bribery, recover stolen assets, and align tax anti-money laundering and anti-corruption frameworks into a more coherent global system. Ladies and gentlemen, at a time of fiscal stress, rising inequality, and growing pressure on multilateral cooperation, improving financial integrity is both a matter of fairness and of collective resilience. It is indispensable domestic resource mobilization to deliver the 2030 agenda. The resources to finance a better world exist. They are simply in the wrong place. It is our collective responsibility to bring them back, back to the classrooms, the clinics, and the communities that need them the most. Let us ensure that this special meeting marks a turning point from commitments to implementation, and from ambition to measurable impact. Let me in the end acknowledge the excellent collaboration with UNODC in preparing this meeting, and let me also convey DESA's deep commitment to all Member States in ensuring that severe commitment is translated into concrete reforms and tangible results. Thank you, Mr. President.

I thank the ASG for Economic Development for this closing remark. And now I will deliver my closing remarks. ASG, with Hanif, Excellencies, distinguished delegates, colleagues, as we conclude this first ever ECOSOC Special Meeting on Financial Integrity, I would like to appreciate the openness, the depth and constructive spirit with which we have this discussion today. In the first segment, we examined global coordination and norm setting. The second segment drew attention to capacity gaps in investigations, in prosecutions, and in judicial capacities, as well as the potential of innovation to strengthen enforcement. Across the discussions, There was a clear understanding among member states and experts that strengthening financial integrity is not solely a technical exercise, nor can it be addressed within silos. It is a systemic challenge requiring coordination across policy domains and over time across institutions and across borders. Several cross-cutting messages stood out. First, integration matters. Fragmented approaches across tax, financial intelligence, customs, anti-corruptions, and law enforcement frameworks, often operating under different mandates, standards, and timelines, weaken outcomes. Second, capacity building must be demand-driven and context-specific. Greater access to data and standards needs to be accompanied by institutional, legal, and financial capacities to support their effective use, including for investigation, persecutions, and recovery. Third, financial integrity is inseparable from development outcomes and from today's geopolitical realities. in the context of fiscal stress and eroding trust in multilateralism. Weaknesses in financial integrity directly constrain domestic resource mobilization and undermine public confidence in institutions, particularly in countries facing significantly capacity constraint. Third, the Special Meeting also speaks directly to the vision guiding ECOSOC's 2026 session under the motto, delivering better. Today's discussions have brought forward ideas for more coherent policy implementation, system-wide advances to policy and its implementations. Excellencies, the SOBIAC commitment recognize illicit financial flows, financial integrity, and transparency as core elements of the financing for development framework. Today's meeting gives effect to the Savoye commitment mandate to convene a special meeting of ECOSOC on financial integrity, providing a platform for systemic dialogue on illicit financial flows and promoting coherence across anti-corruption, anti-money laundering, and international tax cooperation forums. Looking ahead, the mandate entrusted to ECOSOC calls for sustained engagement. ECOSOC has decided to hold this meeting annually. And while I will not chair next year's meeting, of course, I keenly look forward to it. I would also like to invite all the delegations and stakeholders to the 2026 ECOSOC special meeting on international cooperation in tax matters. to be held on 27th of March. That meeting will focus on implementing the SOVIA commitment actions on international tax cooperation, advancing discussions on modernizing nexus rules in a digital economy, and harnessing artificial intelligence responsibly in tax administrations. Also, upcoming ECOSOC subsidiary body, the Commission on Crime Prevention and Criminal Justice, is in the midst of preparing for the 15th Crime Congress, which will be held in April in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates. The discussions held today will be reflected in a President's Summary and will help inform future deliberations across the international systems including the April ECOSOC Financing for Development Forum, negotiations on international tax cooperation, and efforts under the United Nations Convention against Corruptions and other relevant implementation processes. Together, these discussions will further strengthen efforts towards achieving the Sustainable Development Goals. Excellencies, Let me conclude by thanking all our keynote speakers, panelists, respondents, delegations, and key stakeholders for their substantive contributions. Strengthening financial integrity requires your political leadership and long-term commitment. As ICOSAC marks its 80th anniversary, I call for active engagement from all the member states and stakeholders. ECOSOC stands ready to play its part, and together we can build on today's momentum to meet the challenges ahead with courage, with solidarity, and with purpose. I thank you. With this, the meeting is adjourned. Thank you.
